newsitem.title: USA: Vice President Gore, rival Kemp trade dinner jokes.
newsitem.headline: Vice President Gore, rival Kemp trade dinner jokes.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore and Republican challenger Jack Kemp met on Thursday night for the first time since their debate last week and traded self-deprecating jokes before an audience of cardinals, clerics and New York political figures.

The setting was the annual New York Archdiocese dinner honouring Al Smith, the first Roman Catholic to run for the presidency, and the evening ended with the two men patting each other on the back -- like the old friends they are.

The dinner's board made headlines last August by breaking with a tradition they had followed during every presidential election year since 1960 and declining to invite the presidential candidates. Instead they invited the vice presidential rivals.

The gesture was seen as a snub directed at President Bill Clinton by New York's fiercely anti-abortion cardinal, John O'Connor. He later said in a local TV interview that he thought it was wise that Clinton not come because of his veto of the bill banning late-term abortions.
O'Connor remained silent Thursday night when asked by a reporter if he had snubbed Clinton.

But there was no sign of friction between him and Gore at the dinner, a major New York political event attended by the state's governor, two senators, the city's mayor, two former mayors, two cardinals and scores of prominent New York Catholics.

Kemp took stage centre first and declared: "My friend Al Gore has set a new standard for the office of vice president. No other vice president in American history has been forced to remain loyal while his president switched parties in the middle of his term."

Gore looked on in disagreement but then burst into laughter as Kemp said: "What has he done for me in return? Why in ... our debate the other night he resorted to the lowest, dirtiest, most unconscionable trick in the political book. He called me a nice guy.

"For four days after the debate I read headlines like 'Kemp no match for Gore's debating skill,' 'Kemp unwilling to challenge Clinton on character' and 'Kemp: Too nice to be president,'" he said. "Can you think of worse headlines for a politician?"
Gore gave as good as he got, saying, "Remember when people were saying there were too many insults in politics. After our debate, they were saying, 'Why can't we have insults?'"

He saved the worst insults for himself by mocking his now-famous wooden speaking manner and doing a slide show that celebrated the obscurity of past vice presidents and their failure to leave a mark on history.

"I am tired of all those stiff jokes like 'Al Gore is so stiff that racks buy their suits from him' and 'Al Gore is an inspiration to those millions of Americans who suffer from Dutch Elm disease,'" he said.

He borrowed a technique from the films "Zelig" and "Forrest Gump" that inserted him into various famous historical scenes like winning the pennant for the New York Yankees and wearing a space suit while orbiting the earth.

The last doctored photograph was the funniest. Declaring that he and Bill Clinton go way back, he showed the famous photograph of a teenage Clinton shaking President John Kennedy's hand in 1963. There in the audience was Al Gore. "We had quite a day," Gore intoned.
